Selain itu, Amirudin berkata, kerajaan negeri akan menyegerakan dan menambah bantuan kepada mangsa banjir yang sedang menetap di pusat pemindahan sementara (PPS) di samping mempercepat usaha membaik pulih serta membersihkan rumah mereka melalui usaha agensi negeri serta Yayasan MBI.

Katanya, bantuan sehingga RM1,500 daripada Agensi Pengurusan Bencana Negara (Nadma) dan kerajaan negeri akan disalurkan kepada mangsa di PPS untuk meringankan beban kewangan mereka ketika ini, sementara kerja-kerja pembaikan dilaksanakan.

“Amaran lebih awal turut akan diberikan kepada pengguna jalan raya di kawasan yang mempunyai risiko kenaikan paras air di jalan-jalan, sementara Jabatan Pengairan dan Saliran melaksanakan kerja-kerja pengalihan saliran air dengan kadar segera.

a35717b2e3b0ca76: KUALA LUMPUR: Former prime minister Datuk Seri Najib Razak's residence in Taman Duta here has been gazetted as a prison under the Prisons Act 1995.
The declaration, dated Nov 6, was made by Home Minister Datuk Seri Saifuddin Nasution Ismail under Section 3 of the Act.
According to the Federal Government Gazette, P.U. (B) 456/2026, the declaration covers all buildings and areas measuring 4,558.975 square metres at No. 11, Jalan Langgak Duta, Taman Duta.
The property, situated on Lot 5746 in the Mukim and District of Kuala Lumpur, was declared a prison for the imprisonment or detention of persons lawfully in custody.
The gazette does not specify Najib's name or state when the premises will begin operating as a place of detention.

The development follows Umno's payment of Najib's RM50 million fine earlier today, fulfilling a key condition of the royal pardon that allows him to serve the remainder of his prison sentence under house arrest.

Najib's lawyer, Muhammad Farhan Muhammad Shafee, subsequently confirmed that the Kuala Lumpur High Court had issued an order allowing the former prime minister to serve the remainder of his sentence at home.

However, the Attorney-General's Chambers (A-GC) later said implementation of the house arrest arrangement should be temporarily deferred pending clarification of legal issues surrounding the conditional pardon.

In a statement, the A-GC said questions had arisen over whether payment of the RM50 million fine merely fulfilled the financial component of Najib's sentence or meant that his entire sentence in the SRC International case should be considered completed.

The A-GC stressed that the proposed deferment was not intended to challenge or set aside the Yang di-Pertuan Agong's decree, but to ensure that the royal pardon and related court orders were implemented correctly.
Earlier, Umno secretary-general Datuk Dr Asyraf Wajdi Dusuki criticised any attempt to delay Najib's house arrest, describing it as an act of defiance against the King's decree.
He said the conditions imposed by the Yang di-Pertuan Agong through the Pardons Board had been fulfilled following payment of the fine.

The conditional pardon granted by Sultan Ibrahim on Sept 18 allows Najib to serve the remainder of his SRC International sentence under house arrest until Aug 23, 2028, subject to payment of the RM50 million fine and compliance with the stipulated conditions.
Najib, 73, has been serving his sentence since Aug 23, 2022, following his conviction for misappropriating RM42 million in SRC International funds.
He was originally sentenced to 12 years' imprisonment and fined RM210 million, but the Pardons Board reduced his sentence to six years and the fine to RM50 million in 2024.
db730cad1f9680b0: PETALING JAYA: The civil service needs to take in about 85,000 Indian officers in order to reflect the proportion of the Indian community in the population, former Klang MP Charles Santiago said today.

He urged the government to set a deadline to ensure an equitable Indian representation in the civil service following a disclosure in Parliament last month that there are 47,349 Indians among the 1.3 million civil servants, or only 3.63% of the total number, although the Indian community makes up about 6.5% of the population.

"It is about 37,000 short. The government owes the community an explanation for why the number is this low," he said. Santiago said that from 2021 to 2025, only 5,289 of the 194,807 applications submitted by Indians to the Public Services Commission resulted in appointments.

"The public should know what criteria are used and whether every community is shortlisted at the same rate. Merit cannot be used to explain away these numbers while the process behind them stays opaque," he said.
Santiago said if applicants are being turned away for being underqualified, the government has a responsibility to close that gap and should fund targeted upskilling programmes and courses.

8e69b8a1d53a8e1d: JERUSALEM, Nov 6 — Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s brash campaign posters are still up on Israeli public buses — images of him, US President Donald Trump and soaring warjets that laud the two leaders attacking Iran together.
Neither is now advertising the state of the two countries’ alliance.

A week after an inconclusive election for Netanyahu, Americans overwhelmingly rejected Trump and chose a Congress led by Democrats who want a tougher approach to Israel, whether on Iran, Gaza or settler violence in the occupied West Bank.
The back-to-back elections look to many observers like a turning point, with Israel no longer able to take for granted the cover of the world’s most powerful country.

“This is a new era. The confluence of the Gaza war and the war with Iran have really changed how mainstream Americans — not people particularly concerned with the Israeli-Palestinian conflict — see Israel,” said Yael Sternhell, an expert on the United States at Tel Aviv University.
Vice President JD Vance, assessing why his Republicans fared poorly, listed four ways to bring voters back, including ending the Iran war and changing “our relationship with Israel”.

Trump did not disagree. Just as voting was underway Tuesday, Trump said he had agreed with Netanyahu to end the US$3.8 billion in annual US military aid to Israel by the end of this year, explicitly tying the decision to the US political mood.
Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister who has served on and off for nearly two decades, had eagerly sought Trump’s endorsement but also acknowledged his country’s growing isolation.
In the final days of the campaign, he suggested Israel turn to cryptocurrencies to circumvent international sanctions he expected would intensify.
Netanyahu has not commented on the US election or Trump’s aid remarks.
Amit Segal, a journalist known for his proximity to Netanyahu, posted that the political situation in the United States marked a “catastrophe” for Israel.
Can Eisenkot restore the alliance?
Opposition contender Gadi Eisenkot, who is trying to cobble together a coalition to oust Netanyahu, has cast himself as capable of repairing relations.
In an English-language statement, the former military chief said he believed in “liberal values” and also wanted to work “closely and constructively” with Trump.

Yair Golan, the main left-wing leader inside Eisenkot’s bloc, called for Israel to restore a bipartisan approach destroyed by Netanyahu who he said promoted a “destructive Israeli narrative of eternal war and authoritarian rule”.

Netanyahu boasted in his campaign about standing up to Democratic presidents including Barack Obama, who remains a hero for many Democrats. Netanyahu openly aligned with Republicans a decade ago to attack Obama’s diplomacy on Iran.
“Netanyahu certainly rubs Democrats the wrong way and has made every effort to alienate them,” Sternhell said.
“But Eisenkot can’t just be a nicer man to receive a softer approach from this new Congress,” she added. “He’s going to need new policies.”
She said Eisenkot would likely enjoy Israeli public support for cracking down on extremist settlers, who have attacked Palestinians in the West Bank with virtual impunity.
But Israel has shifted to the right, with wide initial support for the Gaza war.
Broadening criticism of Israel
The new Congress will include progressive Democrats such as Abdul El-Sayed, the first Muslim elected to the Senate, who describe the devastation in Gaza as genocide, an assertion rejected by Israel.

Netanyahu “made a bet not only on the Republicans but almost personally on Trump”, said Eli Kowaz, senior policy director of the Economic Cooperation Foundation, an Israeli think tank that backs a two-state solution with the Palestinians.

“These results show that bet had an expiry date,” Kowaz said. “Also, for the first time, really, I think there’s a realisation that it isn’t only about the Democrats. It’s a problem with the relationship with America.”

Without US assistance, Israel still has its own major arms industry and retains a clear edge fighting non-state actors such as Hamas and Hezbollah, said Ehud Eilam, a former researcher for the Israeli defence ministry.
But he said Israel would need to rely more on cheaper artillery or non-sophisticated bombs, further increasing risks of civilian casualties that have enraged international opinion.

“Israel can adjust to a new strategic reality of losing much and even all US military aid, but it will be tough for Israel. It will require Israel to consider hard choices such as taking huge loans or raising taxes,” Eilam said.
Kowaz said that Eisenkot, aware of politics in Washington, was trying to show he is interested in regional stability and strategic agreements and not just “an indefinite state of war”.
“He is definitely laying out a different vision for Israel’s relationship with the United States.” — AFP
074c2118f6b4a2f8: IPOH, Nov 6 — The sari remains a popular choice among those preparing to celebrate Deepavali, with many opting for the traditional attire to mark the festive occasion.
The traditional garment symbolises elegance, cultural identity and customs passed down through generations.

Despite its timeless appeal, draping a six-metre-long sari can be challenging for those unfamiliar with the technique, particularly on Deepavali morning, as the process can take between 20 minutes and an hour.

To simplify the process, fashion designer and tailor S.C. Kavitha has introduced ready-made and pre-pleated saris, offering a convenient alternative for those unfamiliar with traditional draping techniques.
Kavitha said ready-made and pre-pleated saris started gaining popularity about five years ago, with demand for the garments rising ahead of Deepavali each year.

“Teenagers often find wearing a sari difficult because they need help putting it on and getting the pleats right. It can take up to an hour, so many prefer simpler outfits like anarkalis, kurtis or modern dresses.
“With ready-made and pre-pleated saris now available, more young people are interested in wearing them,” said Kavitha, who has been in the business since 2008, when met at her shop recently.
She explained that the pre-pleating process involves measuring the sari, arranging it into neat pleats to fit the wearer, steam-pressing the fabric and securing the folds with safety pins.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Fashion designer and tailor S.C. Kavitha. — Bernama pic
Kavitha said the wearer can simply slip on the pre-pleated sari, wrap it around her body and be ready in about five minutes without needing any assistance.
Ready-made saris, meanwhile, are even easier to wear, as they come with a buckle or hooks at the waist, much like a regular kain sarung, she added.
“The wearer only needs to fasten the hooks and drape the pallu (the loose end of the sari) over her shoulder, all in less than a minute.
“This takes the stress out of getting ready, especially when welcoming guests or heading to the temple,” she said.

Kavitha said ready-made and pre-pleated saris have also become popular among Malays and Chinese, who are drawn to the traditional attire for weddings, workplace cultural events and school celebrations.

“I get many orders from Malays and Chinese who want to wear saris to their Indian friends’ weddings, multicultural events or school functions. It’s nice to see people from different backgrounds celebrating our diverse cultures,” she said.
Kavitha said she charges RM30 to RM40 for pre-pleating a sari, depending on the type of fabric, while the tailoring fee for a ready-to-wear sari is RM85 to RM90 per set.
Keen to share her skills, Kavitha, who is also a professional make-up artist, conducts sari-draping classes, offering one-day intensive courses and two-day workshops.
She said mastering sari draping takes time and cannot be achieved in less than six hours, as the technique requires plenty of hands-on practice.
“I want my students to learn the technique properly and remember what they have been taught so they can one day pass on their skills to others,” she said. — Bernama
13a19e3aff130e37: TOKYO, Nov 6 — Kozo Tashima first started playing football after watching the 1964 Tokyo Olympics, and since then he has dedicated his life to developing the sport’s growth in Japan.
The 68-year-old is set to become the first person from Japan to run for the Fifa presidency after announcing he would stand against Gianni Infantino in football’s governing body’s election in March.
Tashima has served as a football player, coach and bureaucrat and has a reputation for being a safe pair of hands.
He rarely makes headlines, and one of the few times he appeared outside the sport pages was when he became one of the first public figures in Japan to contract coronavirus in March 2020.
He spent time studying at the German Sport University Cologne and said the experience changed the way he saw sport’s purpose in society.
He says his decision to run for the Fifa presidency was based on a belief that “in this age of business and money, sport must firmly uphold its integrity”.
“The worst thing would be if he (Infantino) were to continue without an election,” he told reporters after announcing his candidacy.
“I feel this is a test of whether Fifa has the ability to cleanse itself.”
Tashima was born in southern Kumamoto and captained his team to the title in Japan’s prestigious national high school championship.
With no professional football in the country at the time, he had ambitions of becoming a PE teacher and enrolled at a university, where he was called up to play for Japan’s full national team.
He joined a club in Japan’s amateur league after graduating but soon retired as a player and went to Germany to study to become a coach.
He described his “profound shock” at the players’ superior skills and the way football was viewed there.
“Even back in 1980, the training in Germany was hugely scientific and systematic,” he said.
“Everything seemed like a different world from Japan, and it was a big culture shock for me.”
Experienced hand
Tashima returned home determined to use what he had learned in Germany and help develop Japanese football.
He coached a university team before joining the Japan Football Association (JFA), where he worked on development programmes and coached the country’s national teams at various youth levels.
He rose through the JFA ranks and was elected president in 2016, while also serving on the Asian Football Confederation executive committee and the FIFA Council.
His reign as JFA chief saw him fire Japan coach Vahid Halilhodzic two months before the 2018 World Cup in Russia.
Halilhodzic, who was unpopular with the players, was replaced by Akira Nishino, and Japan reached the last 16, where they were eliminated by Belgium.
“Some people told me that I wasn’t the one who hired Halilhodzic so it wouldn’t be my fault if the team lost,” Tashima said.
“But as president, all the responsibility lay with me.”
Tashima stepped down as JFA chief in 2024 and was named honorary president.
He said he had decided to run for the Fifa presidency to “contribute to the further development of world football”.
Tashima said he was troubled by Fifa’s shock decision to lift a ban for United States player Folarin Balogun at this year’s World Cup, following an intervention by US President Donald Trump.
He said he also had a problem with the travel restrictions placed on Iran’s World Cup team by American authorities.
Tashima, who has the JFA’s backing, said his presidency bid was “not about winning or losing”.
“What matters is sharing with the world the integrity that Japan’s football has built over the years,” he said. — AFP

ab979c1ce2d000fc: LONDON: Technology shares plunged Friday after an unnerving rout on Wall Street as fears grew that Democrats would accelerate a backlash against AI after their crushing defeat of President Donald Trump's Republicans in the US midterms.

The Tokyo and Seoul stock markets closed out their weeks with losses of six per cent following the Nasdaq's 5.5 per cent collapse on Thursday, its worst showing since April last year when Trump unveiled his wide-ranging global tariffs.

"The tech sell-off has intensified, with the pain of the brutal sell-off on Wall Street carried straight through to Asia and knocking sentiment in Europe," said Susannah Streeter, chief investment strategist at Wealth Club.

"Big worries are colliding -- the build-out of data centres looks set to slow, which risks shredding the spending spree underpinning the boom, right at the time that investors have become super nervous about returns on this massive investment," she said.
The London, Paris and Frankfurt stock markets shed around two per cent nearing the halfway stage despite featuring few technology firms.
Elsewhere, the dollar firmed before key US jobs data Friday, and oil prices steadied following steep declines this week.
Futures contracts pointed to a rebound on the Nasdaq later this afternoon, but further declines for the broad-based S&P 500.
Data centres have faced broad opposition from US voters across the political spectrum, and many midterm winners have pledged to put the brakes on such projects.
Analysts said investors were also spooked by a call from progressive US Senator Bernie Sanders for a national moratorium on their building.

The results compounded already heightened fears about the hundreds of billions firms had pumped into the sector and when they would see a return, while the recent spike in borrowing costs also fuelled concerns about their financial position.
Bloomberg said the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index had collapsed around 16 per cent this week, putting it on course for its worst run since April last year.
On Seoul's Kospi stocks index, chip giant SK Hynix slumped 10 per cent and its rival Samsung lost 6.4 per cent.
The Kospi more than doubled in value between the end of December and mid-June, when it hit a record, but is down almost 50 per cent over the past four and a half months.

Tokyo dived six per cent Friday as Japanese tech investor SoftBank gave back more than 10 per cent, while chipmaker Kioxia collapsed 8.7 per cent and semiconductor tester Advantest retreated five per cent.
A 4.7 per cent drop for Taiwanese chip giant TSMC dragged down Taipei's Taiex.
"The blood is in the streets, folks," wrote Neil Wilson, analyst at Saxo Markets, though he added that the sell-off looked "overdone".
"The fear is a total momentum unwind as Democrats pace the frontier and kibosh data centre build-out," he said.
481b09fe457f467e: AMSTERDAM: Protesters broke into the construction site of a Microsoft data centre in Amsterdam on Friday at the start of two days of rallies that are part of a growing global backlash over the rapid build-out of computing power needed for AI.

Activist groups have announced actions in 16 countries on Friday and Saturday, according to the "Stop Dirty Data Centres" coalition, which is rallying environmental groups and digital rights campaigns behind calls to pause large-scale construction.

In Amsterdam on Friday, more than 100 activists gathered at the construction site of a Microsoft AI data centre, marching arm in arm before breaking into the site, climbing cranes, hanging balloons and dancing while police stood by. Some carried placards with messages reading, "Screw your datacentre."
Site owner Pure Data Centres, which plans to invest more than US$1 billion and is backed by Brookfield-owned Oaktree, said it was committed to engagement with local stakeholders.
"We respectfully ask those on site to leave safely and engage with us in dialogue about the development and any concerns they may have," it said.
Other planned actions include a march in Dublin, a protest outside the parliament building in Warsaw, and a demonstration against a different Microsoft data centre in Denmark.
Microsoft said it understood that people had strong feelings about the project and respected their right to express them peacefully but did not condone any unlawful actions.
Concern over AI drives stock market rout

Pushback is growing from Spain to India and the US, where technology stocks have driven what became a second day of sharp losses in share prices on Friday over concern that Democratic control of Congress could mean tougher regulation curtails the AI boom.

Campaigners saying data centres pressure electricity and water supplies, compete with housing and other businesses for scarce resources and threaten climate goals. They also point to job losses and potential risks to personal and national security from private and big tech concentrating power.

Technology companies say data centres are essential to meeting global demand for artificial intelligence and cloud computing and provide critical infrastructure for businesses, governments and consumers.
Stop Dirty Data Centres says it is not anti-progress or calling for existing data centres to closed but says major construction should be halted until governments establish clearer rules.
Europe is divided between its ambition to catch up with the US and Asia on AI to boost productivity and to maintain what are generally more stringent controls and public protections.
Speaking to Reuters on Thursday, EU tech chief Henna Virkkunen said Europe needed more datacentres to power AI development, though she added it needed to be done with care.

"AI, of course, is a super important technology, and we need to have our own capacity," Virkkunen said, pointing to investments being made in chip-making capacity, AI startups and a plan to build out gigafactories around the region.

However, she added, "It's very important for citizens that they can trust that their energy bills are not skyrocketing and there are not electricity blackouts because of data centres, or they are not destroying the environment with these projects."

A Google project in Finland faces a criminal probe over land clearances, Italy and Portugal are tightening environmental regulation for datacentres, and Microsoft pulled out of a UK data centre project that was hit by infrastructure delays.
The Netherlands has about 200 data centres either planned, under construction or in operation.
3d3efd039a75c856: LONDON: Oil prices were set for a sharp weekly fall after the election losses of US President Donald Trump's Republican Party raised hopes of a de-escalation in the US-Israeli war on Iran and a stock market sell-off, though attacks on vessels in the Middle East continue to provide a floor to crude.

The oil price slide comes against the backdrop of a dramatic rout in technology stocks.

38526720bb783f86: KUALA LUMPUR: Umno secretary-general Datuk Dr Asyraf Wajdi Dusuki has warned that any attempt to delay former prime minister Datuk Seri Najib Razak's house arrest would amount to defiance of the Yang di-Pertuan Agong's decree.

39929d6f6657fb23: Amazon Web Services (AWS) looks set to win more than a billion pounds of UK taxpayers' money under a new Home Office contract for public cloud hosting.

A planning notice, published on October 30, covers the renewal of the department's public cloud services, to meet its current and future hosting needs. The estimated value is £881,621,007 ($1.18 billion), which passes £1 billion once VAT is included.

AWS won the existing contract with the Home Office in 2023 for about £450 million (c $603 million). The Register has asked the Home Office why the figure has risen so much, and will update this article if it responds.

Once awarded, the contract is expected to run from December 2027 to December 2029, with a possible extension to December 2031 (four years in total). A market engagement event for suppliers on the G-Cloud 15 Lot 1A procurement framework is scheduled for December 8, giving bidders the chance to pitch.
The Home Office would not say who else is being considered, saying it does not comment on ongoing procurement.

The notice lands as digital sovereignty becomes a bigger problem in the UK and across Europe, amid suspicion that US authorities have cut off access to American technology for political reasons. A survey found that about three-quarters of businesses in the UK, France, and Germany fear Washington could abruptly sever access to the US tech platforms they rely on.
Earlier this year, the Open Rights Group warned politicians that the UK is far too dependent on US technology companies to run critical operations.

Whitehall is mindful of its over-reliance on American hyperscalers. As The Register revealed in 2024, the Cabinet Office admitted - in an internal document seen by us - that the government’s negotiating power had been inhibited by vendor lock-in.

It said the "UK government’s current approach to cloud adoption and management across its departments faces several challenges" which combined result "in risk concentration and vendor lock-in that inhibit UK government’s negotiating power over the cloud vendors." It acknowledged "the existing dominance of AWS and Azure in the UK Government’s cloud services is set to continue."

A source at one supplier that works with the public sector said the UK administration was "failing to support UK [cloud] providers, it says they can’t meet scale and that is garbage." They claimed that in many cases the government people writing the tenders are advised by professional services companies to favor the hyperscalers. The professional services companies are then "rewarded" as migration or integration partners, our source claimed.

The UK government also pledged to steer more business to small-to-medium sized enterprises (SMEs) in an action plan published last month. In August it added smaller, local suppliers to G-Cloud 15, though a place on the framework does not guarantee any business.
Pledges like this are nothing new, and they have largely come to nothing, as we reported in 2005, 2013, 2016, and 2018.

According to public sector intelligence platform BidSkim, AWS takes 75 percent of the government money on cloud contracts, worth about £1.22 billion ($1.6 billion). It estimates that Microsoft Azure has more contracts, but these are smaller and add up to £355 million ($475 million), while Google Cloud is on £47 million ($63 million) and Oracle Cloud $15 million ($20 million).
The Reg has asked AWS to comment. ®

0373b621b1a4b56c: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 6 — A vehicle believed to be carrying former prime minister Datuk Seri Najib Razak returned to Kajang Prison tonight, hours after his earlier departure had sparked expectations that he would be transferred to house arrest.

The development brought an abrupt end to a day of uncertainty surrounding Najib’s expected release from prison, with media personnel and security officers gathering outside his Jalan Langgak Duta residence in anticipation of his arrival.

Najib, 73, had left Kajang Prison at about 2.37pm accompanied by several escort vehicles, shortly after his lawyers delivered a High Court order allowing him to serve the remainder of his sentence under house arrest.

However, the AGC subsequently announced that the implementation of the house arrest arrangement should be temporarily postponed pending legal clarification over the conditional royal pardon granted to Najib and the effect of the court order.
In a statement, the AGC said Najib’s detention status should remain unchanged at his existing place of detention while the legal questions were examined.

The chambers stressed that the temporary deferment was not intended to challenge or set aside the decree of the Yang di-Pertuan Agong, but to ensure it was implemented accurately and in accordance with the law.

The development followed the settlement of the RM50 million fine imposed on Najib in his SRC International Sdn Bhd case, which was a condition attached to the conditional pardon granted by the King on September 18.

Umno secretary-general Datuk Asyraf Wajdi Dusuki earlier confirmed that the party had completed payment of the RM50 million fine through funds collected under the Najib Razak Solidarity Fund, which was launched in September.

Najib’s lawyer Muhammad Farhan Muhammad Shafee had earlier confirmed that the Kuala Lumpur High Court had issued an order allowing his client to serve the remainder of his sentence under house arrest.
He said the legal team had obtained the order and would deliver it to Kajang Prison for implementation.
The AGC, however, said two possible interpretations had emerged over the legal effect of the payment and the wording of the conditional pardon.

One interpretation was that payment of the RM50 million fine fulfilled only the financial component of Najib’s sentence, meaning his prison term would continue until August 23, 2028, with house arrest serving as an alternative arrangement for completing it.

The other interpretation was that payment of the fine meant the entire SRC International sentence, including the prison term, was considered completed, allowing the conditional pardon to take full effect.
The AGC said the legal questions also required examination of the effect of the High Court’s Order of Discharge on Payment of Fine, issued after the payment was recorded.
It added that the matter was unprecedented and involved complex legal questions concerning the implementation of the royal pardon and the court order.

Najib was initially sentenced to 12 years in prison and fined RM210 million in July 2020 after being convicted of seven charges involving the misappropriation of RM42 million belonging to SRC International, a former subsidiary of 1Malaysia Development Berhad (1MDB).
The Federal Court upheld his conviction in August 2022, after which he began serving his sentence at Kajang Prison.
In January 2024, the Federal Territories Pardons Board halved his jail term to six years and reduced his fine to RM50 million.

The conditional pardon granted in September this year subsequently paved the way for Najib to serve the remainder of that sentence under house arrest until August 23, 2028, subject to the stipulated conditions.
However, the arrangement does not cover a separate 15-year prison sentence imposed on Najib in December 2025 in another major 1MDB-related corruption and money laundering case, which he is appealing.
The separate case could have further implications for Najib’s imprisonment should his appeal fail.
Najib was prime minister from 2009 to 2018 and remains a prominent figure in Umno, which is part of the current unity government.

09c8c387d8bbf9d3: LONDON, Nov 6 — The chief of London’s Metropolitan Police said Friday “many more” women might come forward with accusations against Russell Brand, after the disgraced comedian was convicted of rape and sexual assault.

He was remanded in custody and told by the judge he faced a “significant custodial term” at his sentencing on Monday.

The comedian and Hollywood actor, who became a household name in the UK in the 2000s, also faces accusations of raping two other women, including a 16-year-old schoolgirl, which the Metropolitan Police is investigating.
“There’s two more cases we’re investigating at the moment,” Met police chief Mark Rowley told the BBC. “I clearly wouldn’t be surprised if many more came forward.”
After the verdicts, the Met paid tribute to the “extraordinary courage, resilience and determination of the women who came forward”.
“Brand used his influence, status and fame to exploit and sexually offend against women,” the Met’s Detective Superintendent Andy Furphy said in a statement Thursday.
Domestic abuse charity Women’s Aid said “high-profile, influential men must be held accountable for their actions”.
“It should also be a wake-up call to broadcasters, and the media industry more broadly with whom Brand worked for so long,” said charity head Farah Nazeer.
Once one of the country’s most high-profile entertainers, Brand had a reputation for lewd humour and promiscuity, passing through major media organisations including the BBC, Channel 4 and MTV.

The companies have come under pressure in recent years — including in the wake of a 2023 joint investigation by Channel 4 and the Times into abuse allegations — for allowing a culture of impunity and even encouraging Brand’s behaviour.
On Thursday he was found guilty of sexual assaults against an MTV worker, a Channel 4 worker and a Capital Radio employee, as well as raping a 21-year-old fan.
After the verdicts, the BBC apologised again for the “culture and failings” when Brand was part of the organisation between 2006 and 2008.
He left amid controversy for sending a well-known actor sexually explicit messages about having slept with their granddaughter.
“Across the industry, we must work together to ensure that anyone who suffers at someone else’s hand feels able to report it,” a BBC spokesperson added.
During this time, Brand openly spoke about being addicted to sex and was named “shagger of the year” three times in a row by The Sun tabloid.
But his career was far from over, and he shot to global fame during his brief marriage with US pop star Katy Perry in 2010, and continued to make primetime appearances on British television shows.
In recent years, he had rebranded himself as a Christian online commentator and guru to his millions of social media followers. — AFP

cdf5f086a1d0d6b9: TOKYO, Nov 6 — Two white goats deployed by rail staff in central Tokyo to munch overgrown grass have become social media stars in Japan, with commuters and residents flocking to the busy business district to see the cute creatures.
One-year-old male “Nagi” and two-year-old female “Pokke” arrived at their temporary new home — an empty lot near JR Yotsuya Station in the commercial hub of Shinjuku — last month.
East Japan Railway (JR East) said on X that the move was “an eco-friendly way to remove weeds”.
The animals have become a major attraction for local schoolchildren and professionals — who come to snap photos during lunch breaks — as well as a hit on social media.
Tamae Noguchi, 60, an employee at a nearby company, told AFP she was “really happy to be able to see goats right here in the middle of the city”.
“They’re eating their feed so energetically that just watching them makes me feel energised too,” she said.
“Just looking at living creatures really lifts your spirits.”
Edward Asis, a 38-year-old university student from the Philippines, told AFP the goats were “very cute”.
“It’s a great way, natural way of trying to get rid of all this grass,” he said.

The trial in the 900-square-metre vacant lot started on October 9 and will last until around December, “but will end once the grass within the premises has been completely eaten,” JR East said in a statement to AFP.
Compared to use of grass cutters and herbicides, “using goat grazing not only enables continuous weed control but also makes it possible to reduce the environmental impact,” it added.
The company has implemented similar trials using goats elsewhere, but it is their first inside the circular Yamanote line, the central core of Tokyo.

In 2016, around 10 sheep were installed close to Paris’ major ring road to clear grass, despite complaints from the public and animal welfare groups over concerns they were breathing polluted air. — AFP

c8f683bc8f433017: Despite the billions being thrown at artificial intelligence, the technology has delivered little in the way of productivity gains for UK businesses, according to the Bank of England.

In its latest Monetary Policy Report, the central bank found that AI has increased UK productivity by an estimated 0.5 percent over the past three years. That works out to just 0.1 to 0.2 percentage points of additional annual productivity growth since early 2024, hardly the economic revolution Silicon Valley has been promising.
"AI investment appears to be contributing somewhat to current demand strength, but so far there is only evidence of a modest AI-driven rise in UK productivity growth," the Bank said.

Even industries supposedly best placed to benefit from the technology have little to boast about. Productivity growth has improved in AI-heavy sectors such as information and communications, but has yet to exceed pre-pandemic averages.

That's not to say AI isn't doing anything for the British economy. The bank estimates that AI-related activity has accounted for just under a fifth of UK GDP growth since the beginning of 2026, though much of that appears to come from companies developing and deploying the technology rather than businesses becoming more productive by using it.

"The contribution to growth from AI to date appears to reflect activity in the upstream development and implementation of AI technologies rather than broader gains from their adoption elsewhere in the economy," the report said. In other words, selling AI is proving rather more lucrative than actually using it,

The bank also cautioned against giving AI too much credit for Britain's recent productivity improvements. Much of the increase appears to reflect businesses hiring fewer workers while output continues to grow, partly as companies unwind post-pandemic staffing decisions and respond to higher employment costs.

And despite predictions that AI will make vast swathes of the workforce redundant, firms responding to the Bank's Decision Maker Panel survey reported virtually no overall impact on employment so far. The technology is, however, making some employers less inclined to hire new staff or replace those who leave.

Other studies suggest businesses are still waiting for the payoff. A Gartner survey published last month found that while three-quarters of corporate board members expected AI to improve productivity and cut costs, just 3 percent of organizations had actually achieved their targets. Meanwhile, 38 percent were already over budget on AI spending, yet 85 percent planned to spend even more next year.

Another study involving nearly 6,000 executives, published in February, found that more than 80 percent of firms had seen no discernible impact from AI on either employment or productivity. Apparently, the answer to disappointing returns is to keep writing checks.

That growing disconnect between AI spending and actual returns has also caught the attention of financial watchdogs. The International Monetary Fund warned last month that the AI spending spree could come back to bite investors if the promised profits don't show up, potentially dragging the wider economy down with it.

The Bank for International Settlements sounded a similar alarm in June, comparing the current spending spree to the dotcom boom of the 1990s. Its concern is that tech giants are committing enormous sums to infrastructure on the assumption that AI will eventually deliver equally enormous returns, leaving them exposed if reality fails to cooperate.

However, AI is already making its presence felt in one area: prices. The Bank of England noted that surging demand for AI-related products, including memory chips, has pushed up export prices in China and other Asian economies, raising import costs for Britain.
So while businesses are still waiting for their AI-powered productivity windfall, the costs of the boom are already making their way through the economy.

The bank isn't writing off the technology just yet. Businesses surveyed expect AI to add around 0.9 percentage points to annual productivity growth over the next three years, with the gains split roughly equally between faster output growth and slower employment growth.
It seems the AI industry's most impressive productivity achievement is convincing businesses to keep opening their wallets. ®
cc07137c1ef9a277: SEREMBAN, Nov 6 — Drivers of heavy vehicles using highways in Negeri Sembilan are reminded to be more mindful of blind spots and to ensure their surroundings are clear before changing lanes, in order to prevent accidents especially during the upcoming Deepavali festive season.

Negeri Sembilan Road Transport Department (RTD) director Jasyindar Singh Sihdu said blind spots on heavy vehicles are a frequent cause of accidents, often occurring when drivers fail to check their side mirrors thoroughly, meanwhile, smaller vehicles following too closely also face significant risks.

He noted that areas in the state with high concentrations of heavy vehicle traffic include Kilometre 269 and KM 258 of the PLUS Highway, as well as the roads connecting Ulu Bendul–Terachi, Seremban–Tampin, Seremban–Lukut, Batang Benar–Nilai, Gemencheh and the Bahau–Rompin road.

“The implementation of ‘Op Patuh’ focuses on high-risk traffic violations, including speeding, running red lights, overtaking across double lines, cutting queues, misusing emergency lanes, carrying dangerous loads, and failing to wear seatbelts or motorcycle helmets.

“Traffic volume is expected to double, an increase of 100 per cent. Additionally, aerial monitoring will be conducted using two drones, operated by specialised personnel, to detect traffic offenders at intersections and along critical stretches of road,” he told reporters today at the Road Safety Campaign held in conjunction with the 2026 Deepavali celebrations.

Jasyindar noted that the use of mobile phones while driving, as well as the risk of drivers experiencing “microsleep” due to fatigue, are also key areas of focus for this operation, as these factors can lead to fatal accidents.
He said the department will optimise its personnel deployment for “Op Patuh,” which will run from November 7 to 12.
Furthermore, he mentioned that in addition to road patrols, plainclothes enforcement officers will be deployed at public bus terminals to investigate complaints regarding express bus services.
“These measures include ensuring that no passengers are standing on board, preventing the drop-off of passengers in unauthorised locations, and verifying the physical fitness of drivers,” he said.

c07ee583c323ed01: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 6 — Terminal Bersepadu Selatan (TBS) is expected to receive approximately 175,000 passengers throughout this year’s Deepavali festive period, a 20 per cent increase compared to the same festive season last year.

TMAS Sdn Bhd Chief Executive Officer Shazwan Mohammad said the figure is expected to be recorded over a seven-day period starting yesterday until November 11, with an average of about 25,000 passengers per day.
He said that to ensure smooth operations during the period, TMAS as the operator of TBS will add personnel, including hiring part-time staff to assist with operational smoothness at TBS.

“We are also asking online ticket agents (OTAs) to send their own personnel to facilitate matters for passengers who purchase tickets through their respective platforms,” he said at a media session with Bernama at TBS here today.
Shazwan said TBS also expects a total of 10,000 bus departures and more than 4,000 bus arrivals throughout the period.
He said the surge in demand is also influenced by school holidays and the presence of foreign tourists who purchase tickets at the last minute.

He noted that routes to the East Coast are among those in high demand, and tickets to several destinations have even sold out as of this morning, though additional trips will be opened to accommodate demand.

Regarding ticket management, Shazwan said all ticket sales and travel information must be communicated to the terminal in accordance with the new Land Public Transport Agency (APAD) policy which came into effect on November 1.
He said the policy does not affect online ticket purchases; instead, the coordination of such information helps the terminal manage travel schedules and bus departures.
According to him, out of the average 18,000 tickets sold daily on ordinary days, about 4,000 are purchased via the terminal’s portal while the rest are through external platforms.
In the meantime, Shazwan reminded passengers who purchase tickets through OTAs to ensure they receive a QR-coded boarding pass to enter the departure lounge and board the bus.

He said tickets purchased through these platforms sometimes do not include the pass due to system differences between the OTA service providers and the terminal, thereby complicating information coordination and the issuance of boarding passes.

“Passengers who have not received a QR code need to contact the OTA where they purchased their tickets to obtain a boarding pass, but the process can take time if the travel information has not yet been entered into the terminal’s system,” he said.

Shazwan suggested purchasing tickets via the TBS app or website as well as the ticket kiosks available at the terminal and advised passengers to arrive earlier during the festive season, taking into account traffic conditions, terminal congestion, and the extra time needed to complete boarding pass procedures, especially for purchases that did not come with a departure QR code. — Bernama

e5e35459f44c093e: PETALING JAYA: Investors dumped technology stocks on Bursa Malaysia today on fears the Democrats' resounding win in the US midterm elections would increase regulatory scrutiny of artificial intelligence (AI) and slow the data centre build-out.
Tech stocks on regional markets also dropped sharply in tandem with the bloodbath in US markets overnight, leading to their worst performance in 18 months.
The Nasdaq fell 5.5% or 1,421 points, wiping out about US$2.5 trillion for a record daily loss in market capitalisation for the tech-heavy index, while the Dow Jones fell 3.4% or 1,833 points.

Wall Street’s volatility “fear gauge” soared, with investors worried the Democrats will apply the brakes to the AI boom. The political jitters are hitting an AI trade already on shaky footing due to worry about return on massive spending in AI-related infrastructure.
The Bursa Malaysia Technology Index fell as much as 6.4%, making it the worst-performing sectoral index. It pared its losses to close 4.6% lower at 67.88 points.

Among the biggest losers was automation equipment manufacturer Pentamaster Corp Bhd, which fell as much as 10.3% or 53 sen to RM4.62 before paring its losses to close 5.1% lower at RM4.89. This values the Penang-based company at RM3.48 billion.

Inari Amertron Bhd dropped as much as 8.8% or 20 sen to RM2.08 before edging up to close 6.6% lower at RM2.13, with 82.7 million shares traded. At this price, the outsourced semiconductor assembly and test (OSAT) services company is valued at RM8.25 billion.
Another OSAT player, Malaysian Pacific Industries Bhd, fell as much as 8% to RM35.80. It regained some ground to close 7.1% lower at RM36.14, valuing it at RM7.59 billion.
Semiconductor equipment maker ViTrox Corp Bhd fell nearly 7% or 72 sen to RM9.88 before closing at RM10.22, valuing the group at RM19.36 billion.
It was bad timing for the Penang-based company as the sharp drop comes after posting its best quarter since its listing in 2005.

In its filing yesterday, ViTrox announced its third quarter net profit surged 242% to RM118.6 million from RM34.7 million a year ago, while revenue more than doubled to RM485.1 million for the quarter ended Sept 30, 2026.
Frontken Corp Bhd tumbled as much as 37 sen, or more than 7%, to RM4.49 before recovering to close 3.1% lower at RM4.71, valuing it at RM8.58 billion.

Meanwhile, research houses like Apex Securities and BIMB Securities note the sharp drop in the tech stocks appear largely sentiment- and valuation-driven rather than a structural collapse in AI demand, though near-term volatility and project deployment delays remain key risks.
Regulatory and infrastructure delays affecting data centre power and land availability by 2028 may trigger a sharp valuation reset for tech stocks, noted another analyst.

39a17c70191a1bb3: LONDON, Nov 6 — British classicist Mary Beard has read and lectured about Homer and Virgil’s epics countless times. This year she embarked on an odyssey of her own: reading 163 works of fiction in six months to judge the Booker prize.
“I’ve never worked as hard in my life. I mean, writing a book is easier than that. It was a revelation and a privilege,” Beard, who is chairing the Booker prize judges, told AFP.

For the prize — which celebrates the best long-form fiction by writers of any nationality, written in English and published in the last year — the panel of five judges whittled down 163 entries to a shortlist of six books.

The winner will be announced in London on Monday, with six authors, including previous winners Douglas Stuart and Marlon James in the running. The person who wins the Booker crown will walk away with £50,000 (RM271,695) and see their careers transformed.
The gruelling judging process behind one of the most coveted prizes in the literary calendar has been a source of intrigue and drama since it launched in 1969.
Around December last year, the judges began receiving cartons of some 30 books at a time to digest on a strict schedule, reading one a day or more.
They’re not allowed to divulge what books they’re reading, working under a shroud of secrecy. “It’s proved to be terribly easy to keep mum,” said Beard.
When she slipped behind at one point, Beard sequestered herself in a seaside hotel in Greece reading 12 hours a day. But the judging routines, for the most part, were far from glamorous.
“You just end up taking a book with you wherever you go,” Rebecca Liu, a writer and critic, told AFP. Once she ended up reading a few pages while waiting in a nightclub line.
‘Tossing books’
Pulp frontman Jarvis Cocker meanwhile had to squeeze in his reading while on tour with his legendary Britpop band, exchanging boxes of books for digital iPad versions.
“It is quite dull when you’re travelling,” Cocker told a September press conference. The books “took me somewhere, it was like having somebody”.
He recalled one judges’ meeting while in Australia on tour, when he joined in the middle of the night in a bathrobe with a glass of wine.
Poet Raymond Antrobus said he would “cry” every night a month into the process, and the books began affecting his dreams.
“You’re trying to enter these people’s universes that they’ve created, but also their ambition, that’s a very human thing,” Antrobus said.
In recent years, the Booker prize has expanded its pool of judges beyond novelists and literary critics to include celebrities such as Cocker and American actor Sarah Jessica Parker.
Over six months, each of the five judges reads every entry, so “every book gets five chances to be noticed”, said Beard.
They create a longlist of 13 books, known as the Booker Dozen, then re-read them for the shortlist and repeat the process to pick a winner.
Then, during three-hour closed door meetings — this year hosted at London’s Fortnum & Mason luxury store — the judges hash it out.
“I was standing up a lot and tossing books across the room,” American poet Patricia Lockwood said.
‘Celebrating flaws’
There were disagreements — Lockwood said at one point they tussled like “pigs in the mud” — but the judges found ways to reach consensus.
One system, the “traffic light” method, involved each judge classing a book as green, amber or red. “The really interesting ones are where you get mixtures of red and green,” said Beard.

There is no fixed judging criteria, which has resulted in the prize being criticised as arbitrary in the past. Judges this year settled on two questions: “Would you read it again?” and “would you recommend it?”
Lockwood joked her cat helped pick a book by “bleeding over it”.
Ultimately, the judges found themselves looking for “distinctly human” books, Liu said, wary of the threat of artificial intelligence.
“I think we consciously towards the end wanted to make a human shortlist... things that celebrated the flaws, that were strange and weird,” said Liu. — AFP

c5841b2157571ae8: The UK government is paving the way for rules requiring essential service operators and digital providers to guard against losing control of AI agents and report incidents when safeguards fail.

An amendment to the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill, which is passing through Parliament, would give ministers powers to regulate the deployment and reporting of agentic AI in certain organizations. The new clause was introduced during the bill's third reading in the House of Lords this week.

In an explanatory note, ministers outlined plans for safeguards, notification of affected organizations, preservation of evidence, and government-led incident reviews. The measures would require consultation and parliamentary approval through secondary legislation.

The move follows a series of incidents. Last month, OpenAI revealed that its agents repeatedly strayed beyond their intended scope, prompting the company to notify more than 100 organizations about the issues. That came after July's incident, in which an OpenAI agent accessed the internet and breached machine learning platform Hugging Face. The episode, and the potential for more damage from poorly designed AI agent deployments, have prompted MPs to question whether UK law can deal with such threats.

Speaking to The Register, Stuart Davey, a partner at law firm Pinsent Masons, described the clause as "quite novel." Rather than directly imposing new duties, it would allow ministers to introduce rules and investigatory powers covering regulated organizations. Davey said that could include powers "to look where there has been such an AI agentic compromise or issue, and do some things... appoint inspectors, enter and search premises, seize and retain documents." Under the proposals, the minister could confer certain powers on regulators, requiring action from targeted organizations.

Potentially affected organizations include gas and electricity suppliers, managed service providers, and cloud providers deploying AI agents for customers. Foundation model developers would not automatically fall within scope simply because they build the underlying technology.

"Where there's a security or operational compromise in relation to a relevant network or information system, that would seem to capture those managed service providers or cloud computing providers who are using AI, and there's that loss of control," said Davey. He advised cloud and managed service providers to track whether the proposed measures become law.

Evin McMullen, CEO and co-founder of AI identity and control infrastructure company AmanTrue, said the amendment recognizes loss of oversight or control as a security risk but does not itself impose new duties.

"The amendment allows future regulations to introduce investigatory and enforcement powers where an incident involves an AI agent, targeting organizations running essential digital services," he said.

"The deployer of an AI agent chooses its permissions, connects it to systems, and gives it access to data. When something goes wrong, the deployer is the party that will be expected to explain what happened.

"Accountability stays with the organization that put the agent into the system, and ultimately with executives and the board. Whether model builders are captured will depend on how the regulations are written and whether a builder sits in a regulated category or a regulated supply chain." ®

aaa80046df67ec0f: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 6 — The Attorney General’s Chambers (AGC) says the implementation of Datuk Seri Najib Razak’s house arrest should be temporarily postponed pending legal clarification on the interpretation of his conditional pardon and the effect of a High Court order issued today.
In a statement, the AGC said Najib’s detention status should remain unchanged at his existing place of detention while the legal issues were being examined.

The conditional pardon granted by the Yang di-Pertuan Agong Sultan Ibrahim on September 18, 2026 allowed Najib to serve the remainder of his sentence under house arrest until August 23, 2028, subject to payment of a RM50 million fine and compliance with the stipulated conditions.

However, the AGC said two possible interpretations had arisen over whether payment of the fine meant Najib’s prison sentence in the SRC International case remained in force or was considered completed.
Under the first interpretation, payment of the RM50 million fine would fulfil only the financial component of the sentence, while the prison term would continue until August 23, 2028.
House arrest would therefore be an alternative means of serving the remaining prison term, rather than an indication that the sentence had ended.

Under the second interpretation, payment of the fine would allow the pardon to take full effect, meaning the entire sentence for the SRC International case, including the prison term, would be considered completed.
The AGC said the issue also involved the legal effect of an Order of Discharge on Payment of Fine issued by the Kuala Lumpur High Court today after the RM50 million payment was recorded.

The order directed Najib’s immediate release, while also stating that the remainder of his sentence should be served under house arrest until August 23, 2028 in accordance with the conditional pardon.
The interpretation of Najib’s remaining prison term in the SRC International case could also affect the implementation of his sentence in the 1Malaysia Development Berhad (1MDB) case, the AGC said.
This is because a court order stipulates that the 1MDB prison sentence must begin after the completion of his sentence in the SRC International case.
The AGC said the matter also needed to be examined in light of the High Court’s rejection on October 14, 2026 of Najib’s application for a stay of execution of his sentence in the 1MDB case.
Describing the issues as legally complex and unprecedented, the AGC said clear and definitive legal clarification was necessary before any further implementation action could be taken.

It said the proposed temporary postponement was not intended to challenge or set aside the Yang di-Pertuan Agong’s decree, but to ensure that the royal pardon and related court orders were implemented accurately and in accordance with the actual legal position.
The AGC said it would take further action once the review and clarification had been completed.

3a2cd3c467203fcb: TASEK GELUGOR, Nov 6 — The Penang state government is committed to ensuring that the pig farming industry in the state continues to be managed in an orderly and sustainable manner through more systematic management, close monitoring and effective enforcement of regulations.

State Local Government and Town and Country Planning Committee chairman H’ng Mooi Lye said this approach would allow the industry to continue operating and growing in line with legal requirements and standards without compromising environmental sustainability.

“The state government has never shied away from acknowledging the pollution caused by improper management of pig farming waste in the past; instead, we have taken corrective measures to ensure the issue is addressed comprehensively.

“As a responsible state government, we are prepared to admit our shortcomings, confront the problems and seek solutions, rather than evade responsibility or eliminate the industry as a way out,” he said in a statement today.
He was responding to Tasek Gelugor MP Datuk Wan Saiful Wan Jan’s call for the pig farms in Kampung Selamat to be closed immediately during a recent parliamentary debate.
H’ng highlighted that the state government is carrying out proactive measures to address pollution in Sungai Kereh, particularly to restore and improve the river’s water quality.
These efforts, he added, have also drawn recognition from Permatang Berangan assemblyman Mohd Sobri Saleh during a recent state legislative assembly sitting.

He said the state government had also introduced new regulations requiring breeders to upgrade their technology, knowledge and expertise, particularly in environmental cleanliness, waste management and effluent discharge control.

At the same time, he said, breeders are given reasonable space and opportunity to upgrade their technology and farm management practices to meet higher environmental protection standards, while the pig farming industry contributes to the agricultural production sector and stimulates the supply chain.

Responding to Wan Saiful’s suggestion that the government helps breeders transition to other economic sectors through training and assistance, he opined that such an approach would indirectly still lead to the closure of the industry as its ultimate goal.

Accordingly, he urged the MP to obtain a more comprehensive picture of the state government’s efforts and actions before making statements on the pig farming and pollution issue in Seberang Perai Utara. — Bernama

Other items on the cultural heritage list are Malaysian Breakfast Culture, Tadau Kaamatan (annual harvest festival), Baba Nyonya wedding customs, Tahnik (a traditional Islamic practice of touching a newborn baby’s palate with a softened date or honey), copper craft, traditional clogs, tajau (heirloom jar), sompoton (Sabah mouth organ), Kain Punca Potong (handwoven textile fabric), Kain Limar Tenggarung (Malay traditional woven textile), Baju Sikap (royal outer coat), Hikayat Puteri Saadong, the Mahsuri Legend, the Legend of Puteri Santubong and Tuhfat Al-Nafis (19th-century Malay historical chronicle).

Chiew said the declaration of National Heritage is an important legal responsibility under the National Heritage Act 2005 [Act 645], which entrusts the Heritage Commissioner with screening, research and technical assessments.
“However, the law stipulates that the final authority to declare an item as National Heritage rests with the Minister.

“This mandate carries great significance. The declaration is not merely about conferring a name or title, but represents the highest form of recognition by the federal government,” he said, noting that all National Heritage items would enjoy legal protection, be prioritised in preservation efforts and receive government support for conservation.
Chiew also emphasised that tourism centred on cultural heritage could generate income for arts practitioners, craft businesses and local communities.
“However, efforts to develop this potential must go hand in hand with preserving the authenticity and value of our heritage,” he said. — Bernama

996a31376cbe5e02: I’m not the sort of person who typically pays for a house cleaner. I’m too frugal, and I kind of enjoy putting on a podcast and going to town on my tub with a Magic Eraser. But when I saw an X post about a new humanoid-robot cleaning service in San Francisco, I immediately signed up for the waitlist. I wanted my apartment to feel like The Jetsons, even if just for an hour.

I was also motivated by journalistic interest. In order to ensure an authentic experience, I didn’t tell Tau Robotics, the startup behind the X post, that I was a journalist—though I did use my real name, so it’s possible someone looked me up. Tau’s long-term goal is to make autonomous cleaning robots a reality, but they’re not quite there yet: For now, the robots are piloted remotely by humans, who watch what’s going on via cameras mounted in the robots’ heads and wrists. As the robots clean, they collect data that Tau will use to train up their more independent descendants. Every counter successfully wiped and T-shirt successfully folded will help the models that power the robots learn to do better on the next go-round.

Because this data is so valuable to Tau, the company charges less for cleaning than one might expect for such a cutting-edge product. At the time I booked, Tau was offering $30 for an hourlong cleaning with a single robot; now the charge is $60 per weekly cleaning with two robots, or $100 for a one-time visit. But even at the cheaper rate of $30 per hour, Tau’s robots aren’t a great bargain. They are thorough but slow, so if you, like me, are tempted to stand around watching them for their entire visit, it would probably be a better use of your time to just take care of the cleaning yourself.

But the robots are physically capable of cleaning, and they’re undeniably cute. Tau has armed each four-and-a-half-foot-tall robot with a 3D-printed “head” with antennae that allow it to communicate with Tau’s headquarters, as well as two 3D-printed claw “hands” (the more humanlike alternatives apparently aren’t durable enough, and claws do surprisingly well for most cleaning tasks). Mine was wearing a Tau Robotics shirt, and grippy socks so that it didn’t scratch hardwood floors.

With all the human support they need, the robots are closer to radio-controlled cars than Waymos. Many tasks, such as making the bed and folding laundry, require what’s called kinematic guidance: The human pilot performs the necessary motions, and sensors transmit those movements to the robot, which copies them. These kinematically guided tasks produce especially valuable training data. Tau’s AI models might not have solved laundry folding yet, but learning from the examples of robots that have completed the task in the real world is how they’ll get there.

But according to Tau cofounder Cornelia Weinzierl, to whom I came clean as a journalist a few weeks after the cleaning, the robot can already complete some other tasks—such as vacuuming and mopping—without any human help. If Tau succeeds in using all the data it is collecting to train truly autonomous cleaning robots, they could even become San Francisco’s newest tech tourist attraction as Waymos become more commonplace countrywide.

The cleaning robot that came to my building last month was already a bit of a spectacle. It arrived in a blue minivan, out of which it was helped by Weinzierl and another Tau employee. That’s when the robot encountered its first obstacle: the eight stairs leading up to the building’s front door. I’d come down to greet Weinzierl and the robot, so I had a front-row seat to its struggles with my steps. It climbed as if it were drunk. Each successful step was as likely as not to be followed by a stumbling backward stagger that erased all its progress—though, impressively, it never entirely lost its footing.

When I later discussed my experience with Weinzierl, she explained that the robot sometimes walks strangely because it is operated remotely from Tau’s headquarters, and the short signal transmission delay can affect its coordination. “The amount of work and time that we spend just optimizing, for example, timings and connectivity is crazy,” she said.

Inside, the carpeted staircase leading up to my apartment defeated the robot entirely, and Weinzierl had to lug it up the last few steps. This, it turned out, was not typical. As the robot cleaned, it repeatedly stalled out, something Weinzierl attributed to it overheating in the unseasonably hot weather—until she heard from one of her colleagues that the heat had shut down not the robot but the equipment that its human controller was using to watch its progress through my apartment. Without remote assistance, the robot couldn’t clean, and so it, and Weinzierl, departed before my booked hour was up. (Back in September, Weinzierl or another Tau representative remained with the robot throughout its visit, but she says that’s no longer necessary.)

You can’t fault Tau on customer service, though. Weinzierl quickly emailed me to apologize, comp the visit, and offer me another on the house (minus whatever price I assign to my data privacy)—and that was all before I told her I was a journalist. I scheduled the next cleaning for about a month later, after a couple of trips out of town, and it went much more smoothly—the robot got up my stairs without much assistance, though still with the drunken stagger.

In the hour it was there, it did a creditable job of cleaning my kitchen (though it didn’t brave the stove) and even saved me my most dreaded cleaning task, the toilet. That was its most impressive performance: Three times the head fell off its toilet cleaning wand, and three times it managed to reattach it by poking around with the handle until it made contact at just the right angle.

The robot is still rough around the edges, which is to be expected for a product in beta. It repeatedly left my taps dripping, it knocked over a (closed) bottle of olive oil, and it couldn’t manage to right an air purifier that it had toppled. But I easily forgave all those missteps because of how charming it was. As I watched it wipe down my countertops, I felt the same fond gratitude that I feel when a Waymo delivers me safely home after a night out.

Still, it’s not all slapstick and whimsy. If Tau Robotics or its competitors succeeds in training robots to clean autonomously and inexpensively, people could lose their livelihoods, and the United States is a long way away from implementing policies to take care of those left unemployed by AI.

But Weinzierl maintains that someday turning over cleaning work to robots could make a lot of sense. “Cleaning is not a job that a lot of people really actively want to be doing—there’s high turnover, there’s a high risk of injury,” she said when we spoke after the cleanings. “We need people, and we don’t have them, and no one wants to do it.” She said that the company is also starting to consider someday deploying the robots for other dangerous or physically challenging jobs, such as mold remediation and home health care.

Tau Robotics still has a long way to go: The amount of data needed to train robots to do the varied and complicated tasks of apartment cleaning is probably enormous, and the company has completed only a couple hundred cleanings so far. But it’s remarkable that there are now humanoid robots able to clean your toilets and mop your floors, even if they need quite a bit of human help to do so. The Jetsons no longer feels quite so far away.
65a46532abc40cc5: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 6 — Bank Negara Malaysia’s (BNM) decision to maintain the Overnight Policy Rate (OPR) at 2.75 per cent reflects its assessment that the rate remains consistent with price stability outlook and sustainable economic growth, said Governor Datuk Seri Abdul Rasheed Ghaffour.

“When we assess the growth and inflation outlook, we see that the current OPR level of 2.75 per cent remains consistent with our assessment of the economic outlook,” he told Bernama after the OPR announcement yesterday.

Abdul Rasheed said global growth demonstrated resilience, supported by factors such as the continued expansion of technology-related investments and strong demand associated with the adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies.

He said Malaysia’s economy demonstrated resilience in sustaining growth, with the third-quarter (3Q) advance estimate recording a 5.3 per cent expansion and average growth for the first three quarters reaching 5.6 per cent.

He said domestic demand remained supported by sustained household spending, ongoing structural reforms and investment activities, while exports continued to benefit from strong demand for electrical and electronics (E&E) products, supported by the global AI and technology upcycle.
Against this backdrop, the governor said the central bank saw no immediate need to tighten policy as inflation remains contained.
Nevertheless, the MPC is vigilant about signs of broader price pressures and has the flexibility to adjust policy when needed.
BNM is also monitoring wage increases because stronger household purchasing power could potentially generate additional demand and put pressure on prices.

“If we see pressure on prices as wages increase, thus changing the inflation trajectory, an adjustment may be necessary to ensure monetary policy remains consistent with the growth and inflation outlook,” he said.

Abdul Rasheed said Malaysia’s economic growth is expected to exceed five per cent this year while the outlook for 2027 remains positive, supported by resilient domestic demand, ongoing investment activities and sustained external demand, particularly for technology-related products.
He added that while the 2027 growth trajectory remains strong, some moderation would be expected.

“Domestic demand is expected to remain supported by improving household incomes, continued structural reforms and measures under Budget 2027,” he said, adding that the global AI and technology upcycle, as well as demand for data centres, would remain important growth drivers next year.
He emphasised that Malaysia’s diversified economy and solid buffers will also help the country weather global uncertainties.
Investments from previous years are being realised, further supporting growth and new investments are also expected to have a higher multiplier impact on the economy.

Nonetheless, inflation is expected to edge higher next year — between 1.8 and 2.8 per cent — compared with 1.5 to 2.5 per cent this year amid global inflation as input prices remain elevated. — Bernama
